title: OpenMed + privacy-filter NER backends
description:
## Context

OpenMed (github.com/maziyarpanahi/openmed, Apache 2.0) is a medical NLP toolkit with 33+ PII token-classification models and an integration of OpenAI's `openai/privacy-filter` model. Both are directly usable by nym for PII detection beyond regex + GLiNER.

nym currently has two detection paths:
1. **Regex** (`src/engine/patterns.rs`, `src/engine/detector.rs`) — fast, deterministic, no deps
2. **GLiNER NER** (`src/engine/ner.rs`, feature-gated behind `ner`) — zero-shot ONNX model via `gline-rs` + `ort` + `hf-hub`

This epic adds two new NER backends:
- **OpenMed PII models**: Standard HuggingFace token-classification (BIO/BIOES tagging). Small models (33M-82M params) export cleanly to ONNX. Purpose-trained for PII detection on clinical data; will outperform GLiNER for this specific task.
- **OpenAI privacy-filter** (original `openai/privacy-filter` + OpenMed's Nemotron fine-tune `OpenMed/privacy-filter-nemotron`): Custom MoE architecture with Viterbi decoding. More complex but higher quality on structured PII.

## Reference: OpenMed source files to study

All paths relative to github.com/maziyarpanahi/openmed:
- `openmed/core/backends.py` — Backend routing (MLX vs Torch), privacy-filter dispatcher
- `openmed/core/pii.py` — PII extraction pipeline, model family detection, accent normalization
- `openmed/core/pii_entity_merger.py` — Regex-based semantic unit merging with context-aware scoring (Presidio-inspired), validators (SSN Luhn, NPI, phone)
- `openmed/core/pii_i18n.py` — Language-specific patterns and default models
- `openmed/core/decoding/viterbi.py` — BIOES-constrained Viterbi decoder, TokenLabelInfo, transition bias handling
- `openmed/core/decoding/spans.py` — Span post-processing (trim whitespace, tighten email/URL/phone spans)
- `openmed/core/model_registry.py` — Full model catalog with sizes, entity types, confidence thresholds
- `openmed/torch/privacy_filter.py` — PyTorch wrapper for privacy-filter with trust_remote_code
- `openmed/mlx/inference.py` — MLX Apple Silicon path for privacy-filter

## nym codebase map

- `src/engine/mod.rs` — Module exports
- `src/engine/detector.rs` — `Detector`, `DetectorConfig`, `PiiMatch` struct
- `src/engine/patterns.rs` — `PiiPattern`, `PiiCategory`, `Confidence`, regex patterns
- `src/engine/ner.rs` — `NerDetector` (GLiNER), `NerModelConfig`, `NerModelPaths`, smart chunking, entity caching
- `src/engine/replacer.rs` — `Replacer`, `ReplacementStrategy`
- `src/engine/formats.rs` — JSON/structured data handling
- `Cargo.toml` — `ner` feature flag already pulls in `gline-rs`, `ort`, `hf-hub`, `tokenizers`, `ndarray`

title: Evaluate OpenMed PII models for ONNX export
description:
## Goal

Determine which OpenMed PII token-classification models export cleanly to ONNX and benchmark them for nym's use case.

## Background

OpenMed published 33+ PII detection models on HuggingFace. These are standard HuggingFace `AutoModelForTokenClassification` models (BERT-family, ELECTRA, E5, etc.) with BIO/BIOES label schemes. Unlike the OpenAI privacy-filter which uses custom modeling code, these should export to ONNX without issues.

The models we care about are the small ones suitable for CLI use:

| HuggingFace ID | Size | Architecture |
|---|---|---|
| `OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-ClinicalE5-Small-33M-v1` | 33M | E5 (smallest) |
| `OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-SuperClinical-Small-44M-v1` | 44M | DeBERTa-v3 |
| `OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-LiteClinical-Small-66M-v1` | 66M | BERT |
| `OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-FastClinical-Small-82M-v1` | 82M | BERT |

All detect: `first_name`, `last_name`, `email`, `phone_number`, `ssn`, `date_of_birth`, `street_address`

## Steps

1. **Export to ONNX**: For each model, try exporting with `optimum-cli`:
   ```bash
   pip install optimum onnxruntime
   optimum-cli export onnx --model OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-ClinicalE5-Small-33M-v1 /tmp/onnx/clinical-e5-small
   optimum-cli export onnx --model OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-SuperClinical-Small-44M-v1 /tmp/onnx/superclinical-small
   optimum-cli export onnx --model OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-LiteClinical-Small-66M-v1 /tmp/onnx/liteclinical-small
   optimum-cli export onnx --model OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-FastClinical-Small-82M-v1 /tmp/onnx/fastclinical-small
   ```

2. **Record results**: For each model, note:
   - Did export succeed? Any custom ops?
   - ONNX file size (MB)
   - Number of labels in `id2label` (should be BIO/BIOES variants of entity types)
   - Tokenizer type (BERT tokenizer? SentencePiece? Byte-level?)

3. **Quick inference test**: Run each exported model on a test string using Python `onnxruntime`:
   ```python
   import onnxruntime as ort
   from transformers import AutoTokenizer
   
   tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-ClinicalE5-Small-33M-v1")
   session = ort.InferenceSession("/tmp/onnx/clinical-e5-small/model.onnx")
   
   text = "Patient John Smith (DOB: 01/15/1970) called from 555-123-4567 about SSN 123-45-6789"
   inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="np")
   outputs = session.run(None, dict(inputs))
   # Check shape: [1, seq_len, num_labels]
   ```

4. **Recommend a model**: Based on export success, file size, and label coverage, recommend which model to use as nym's default PII backend.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] All 4 candidate models attempted for ONNX export
- [ ] Results table: model, export success, file size, label count, tokenizer type, any issues
- [ ] Inference sanity check passed for at least 1 model
- [ ] Recommendation with rationale for which model to use in nym

## Reference

- OpenMed model registry: `openmed/core/model_registry.py` (search for the model IDs above)
- HuggingFace collection: https://huggingface.co/collections/openmed
- nym's existing ONNX infra: `src/engine/ner.rs` uses `ort` crate + `hf-hub` for downloads

title: Add NER backend trait and routing
description:
## Goal

Create a `NerBackend` trait in nym so multiple NER engines (GLiNER, OpenMed PII, privacy-filter) can be selected at runtime via CLI flag or config.

## Current State

nym has two hardcoded detection paths:
- `src/engine/detector.rs`: `Detector` runs regex patterns (always available)
- `src/engine/ner.rs`: `NerDetector` wraps GLiNER (feature-gated behind `ner`)

The `Detector` in `detector.rs` calls regex patterns and optionally GLiNER in sequence. There's no abstraction for swapping NER backends.

## What to Build

### 1. `NerBackend` trait in new file `src/engine/ner_backend.rs`

```rust
pub trait NerBackend {
    /// Human-readable name for CLI/config
    fn name(&self) -> &str;
    
    /// Entity types this backend can detect
    fn entity_types(&self) -> &[&str];
    
    /// Run detection, returns Vec<PiiMatch>
    fn detect(&self, text: &str) -> Result<Vec<PiiMatch>, Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>>;
}
```

### 2. Wrap existing GLiNER as `GlinerBackend`

Move the core logic from `src/engine/ner.rs::NerDetector::detect()` into a `GlinerBackend` struct that implements `NerBackend`. Keep the smart chunking, entity caching, and deduplication — they stay in GLiNER because other backends may not need them (OpenMed models handle token limits differently).

### 3. `NerBackendRouter` in `src/engine/ner_backend.rs`

```rust
pub struct NerBackendRouter {
    backends: Vec<Box<dyn NerBackend>>,
}

impl NerBackendRouter {
    pub fn new() -> Self;
    pub fn add(&mut self, backend: Box<dyn NerBackend>);
    pub fn detect_all(&self, text: &str) -> Result<Vec<PiiMatch>, ...>;
}
```

`detect_all()` runs all registered backends and merges results. Deduplication uses the same logic as `NerDetector::deduplicate_matches()` — extract that into a shared function.

### 4. CLI integration

Add to `src/main.rs` (or wherever the CLI args are):
```
--ner-backend <NAME>    Select NER backend: gliner, openmed, privacy-filter, all (default: gliner)
```

When `--ner-backend all` is used, all available backends run and results are merged.

### 5. Config integration

Add to `nym.toml`:
```toml
[ner]
backend = "gliner"       # or "openmed", "privacy-filter", "all"
model = "OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-ClinicalE5-Small-33M-v1"  # model-specific override
threshold = 0.5
```

## Files to Modify

- **New**: `src/engine/ner_backend.rs` — trait + router
- **Modify**: `src/engine/ner.rs` — extract `GlinerBackend` impl, keep `NerDetector` as thin wrapper
- **Modify**: `src/engine/detector.rs` — use `NerBackendRouter` instead of direct `NerDetector`
- **Modify**: `src/engine/mod.rs` — export new module
- **Modify**: `src/main.rs` (or CLI module) — add `--ner-backend` flag
- **Modify**: `src/config.rs` — add `[ner]` section parsing

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `NerBackend` trait defined with `name()`, `entity_types()`, `detect()`
- [ ] Existing GLiNER wrapped as `GlinerBackend` implementing the trait
- [ ] `NerBackendRouter` runs 1 or N backends and deduplicates
- [ ] `--ner-backend` CLI flag works
- [ ] Config `[ner]` section parsed
- [ ] All existing tests pass (no behavior change for default GLiNER backend)
- [ ] `cargo fmt` + `cargo test` pass

## Pitfalls

- Don't break the existing `ner` feature gate — `GlinerBackend` must still be `#[cfg(feature = "ner")]`
- The macOS ONNX crash workaround in `ner.rs` must remain — it applies to all ONNX-based backends
- `PiiMatch` struct in `detector.rs` must work for all backends without modification

title: Implement OpenMed PII token-classification backend
Implement OpenAI privacy-filter backend with Viterbi decoding
description:
## Goal

Add a `PrivacyFilterBackend` that implements `NerBackend` and runs the OpenAI privacy-filter model (and its Nemotron fine-tune) with BIOES-constrained Viterbi decoding in Rust.

## Background

The OpenAI privacy-filter (`openai/privacy-filter`) is a custom MoE token classifier that requires:
1. **Custom modeling code** (`modeling_openai_privacy_filter.py` in the HF repo) — this is NOT a standard HuggingFace model
2. **BIOES-constrained Viterbi decoding** with 6 learned transition biases
3. **Span post-processing** to tighten overly greedy boundaries

OpenMed also published a Nemotron fine-tune: `OpenMed/privacy-filter-nemotron`

This is the most complex backend because of the Viterbi decoder and the custom model architecture.

## Reference Implementation (Python)

Study these files from github.com/maziyarpanahi/openmed:

### `openmed/core/decoding/viterbi.py` (~200 lines)
Pure-Python BIOES Viterbi decoder. Key components:
- `TokenLabelInfo`: Resolves `id2label` into BIOES tag/span-label tables
  - `span_class_names`: `["O", "NAME", "EMAIL", ...]`
  - `token_boundary_tags`: `{label_id: "B"|"I"|"E"|"S"|None}`
  - `token_to_span_label`: `{label_id: span_index}`
- `viterbi_decode(token_logprobs, label_info, biases)`: Main decoder
  - Builds start/end/transition score matrices from the 6 biases
  - Runs standard Viterbi with backpointers
  - Enforces BIOES state machine (e.g. B-X can only continue to I-X or E-X)
- `VITERBI_BIAS_KEYS`: 6 learned biases:
  - `transition_bias_background_stay`
  - `transition_bias_background_to_start`
  - `transition_bias_inside_to_continue`
  - `transition_bias_inside_to_end`
  - `transition_bias_end_to_background`
  - `transition_bias_end_to_start`

### `openmed/core/decoding/spans.py` (~80 lines)
- `trim_span_whitespace(start, end, text)` — strip leading/trailing whitespace
- `refine_privacy_filter_span(label, start, end, text)` — tighten spans:
  - For email/URL/phone labels: find strict regex match inside model span
  - For all labels: strip trailing " and" / " or" that model absorbs

### `openmed/torch/privacy_filter.py` (~130 lines)
- Uses `AutoModelForTokenClassification` with `trust_remote_code=True`
- Outputs normalized entity dicts: `{entity_group, score, word, start, end}`
- Calls `refine_privacy_filter_span` on each result

## What to Build

### 1. Rust Viterbi decoder in `src/engine/viterbi.rs`

Direct port of `viterbi.py`. Key structs:

```rust
pub struct TokenLabelInfo {
    pub span_class_names: Vec<String>,
    pub span_label_lookup: HashMap<String, usize>,
    pub token_to_span_label: HashMap<usize, usize>,
    pub token_boundary_tags: HashMap<usize, Option<char>>, // 'B','I','E','S',None
    pub background_token_label: usize,
    pub background_span_label: usize,
}

pub struct ViterbiBiases {
    pub background_stay: f32,
    pub background_to_start: f32,
    pub inside_to_continue: f32,
    pub inside_to_end: f32,
    pub end_to_background: f32,
    pub end_to_start: f32,
}

pub fn viterbi_decode(
    token_logprobs: &[Vec<f32>],  // [seq_len][num_classes]
    label_info: &TokenLabelInfo,
    biases: &ViterbiBiases,
) -> Vec<usize>  // predicted class indices
```

### 2. Span post-processing in `src/engine/span_utils.rs`

Port of `spans.py`:

```rust
pub fn trim_span_whitespace(start: usize, end: usize, text: &str) -> (usize, usize);
pub fn refine_privacy_filter_span(label: &str, start: usize, end: usize, text: &str) -> (usize, usize);
```

### 3. `PrivacyFilterBackend` in `src/engine/privacy_filter_backend.rs`

```rust
pub struct PrivacyFilterBackend {
    session: ort::Session,
    tokenizer: tokenizers::Tokenizer,
    label_info: TokenLabelInfo,
    biases: ViterbiBiases,  // loaded from model config
    threshold: f32,
}

impl NerBackend for PrivacyFilterBackend {
    fn name(&self) -> &str { "privacy-filter" }
    
    fn detect(&self, text: &str) -> Result<Vec<PiiMatch>, ...> {
        // 1. Tokenize
        // 2. ONNX inference -> logits
        // 3. Apply log-softmax to get log-probs
        // 4. viterbi_decode(log_probs, label_info, biases)
        // 5. labels_to_token_spans() -> (label, start, end) triples
        // 6. Map token spans to char offsets
        // 7. Apply refine_privacy_filter_span to each
        // 8. Convert to PiiMatch
    }
}
```

### 4. ONNX export challenge

The privacy-filter uses custom modeling code. Two approaches:

**Option A**: Export to ONNX with `trust_remote_code=True`:
```bash
optimum-cli export onnx --model openai/privacy-filter --trust-remote-code /tmp/onnx/privacy-filter
```
This may or may not work depending on whether the custom ops are ONNX-compatible.

**Option B**: If ONNX export fails, we need to understand the model architecture enough to either:
- Pre-export the ONNX artifacts from Python and host them on HF
- Or use the `candle` crate for native Rust inference

Investigate Option A first.

### 5. Transition bias loading

The 6 Viterbi biases are stored in the model's config.json under keys matching `VITERBI_BIAS_KEYS`. Parse them during construction:

```rust
let biases = ViterbiBiases {
    background_stay: config["transition_bias_background_stay"].as_f64().unwrap_or(0.0) as f32,
    // ... etc
};
```

## Files to Create/Modify

- **New**: `src/engine/viterbi.rs` — BIOES Viterbi decoder
- **New**: `src/engine/span_utils.rs` — Span post-processing
- **New**: `src/engine/privacy_filter_backend.rs` — Backend implementation
- **Modify**: `src/engine/mod.rs` — export new modules
- **Modify**: `Cargo.toml` — add `privacy-filter` feature

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `viterbi.rs` passes unit tests matching OpenMed's Python implementation
- [ ] `span_utils.rs` handles email/URL/phone span tightening
- [ ] `PrivacyFilterBackend` loads model and runs inference on test text
- [ ] Viterbi decoding produces valid BIOES sequences (no B without matching E, etc.)
- [ ] Results match Python implementation on same input (within floating-point tolerance)
- [ ] `cargo fmt` + `cargo test` pass

## Pitfalls

- The privacy-filter model uses `trust_remote_code` — ONNX export may fail or produce custom ops that `ort` can't run. Test this early.
- Viterbi needs `log_softmax` applied to raw logits before decoding — don't forget this step
- The 6 transition biases can be negative — handle sign correctly
- `labels_to_token_spans` must handle gaps in token indices (special tokens like [CLS], [SEP] are skipped)
- This is the hardest backend — if ONNX export fails, escalate early

## Dependencies

- trx-j0p5.2 (NerBackend trait)
- trx-j0p5.1 results (if we learn ONNX export fails for this model, we may need to adjust approach)

title: Port OpenMed smart entity merger for cross-backend dedup
description:
## Goal

Port OpenMed's regex-based semantic entity merger to Rust. This post-processes NER output from ANY backend to merge fragmented predictions into coherent entities.

## Problem

Token classifiers often split semantic PII units across multiple predictions:
```
Model raw output:
  [date] '01' (0.71)
  [date_of_birth] '/15/1970' (0.75)

Expected:
  [date_of_birth] '01/15/1970' (0.73)
```

This happens because tokenizers split strings like `01/15/1970` into sub-tokens and the model may assign different labels to different pieces.

## Reference Implementation

`openmed/core/pii_entity_merger.py` (~350 lines). Key concepts:

### `PIIPattern` struct
Each pattern has:
- `pattern`: Regex for the semantic unit
- `entity_type`: Target label (e.g. "ssn", "phone_number")
- `priority`: Higher = checked first
- `base_score`: Confidence without context (0.01-0.9)
- `context_boost`: Extra confidence when context words found nearby (0.1-0.65)
- `context_words`: Keywords that boost confidence (e.g. ["ssn", "social security"])
- `validator`: Optional function (SSN checksum, Luhn, NPI validation, phone format)

### `merge_entities_with_semantic_units()`
1. Find all regex pattern matches in text
2. For each match, check if it overlaps with model predictions
3. If overlapping: merge fragments, use dominant label (highest cumulative score)
4. If no overlap but high confidence (base + context): add as new entity

### Validators
- `validate_ssn()`: SSN rules (no 000 groups, no 666 area, no 900-999)
- `validate_luhn()`: Credit card Luhn algorithm
- `validate_npi()`: NPI with 80840 prefix Luhn
- `validate_phone_us()`: US phone format checks

### Pattern catalog
- Dates: ISO, US, European, spelled-out months
- SSN: `XXX-XX-XXXX`, `XXX XX XXXX`
- Phone: `(XXX) XXX-XXXX`, `XXX-XXX-XXXX`, 10-digit
- Email: standard pattern
- ZIP: 5-digit, ZIP+4
- Credit card: 4x4 groups with Luhn
- MRN: `MRN:XXXXXX`, `ABX123456`
- Street address: number + street + suffix
- NPI: 10-digit with Luhn

## What to Build

### 1. `PiiMergerPattern` and `PiiMerger` in `src/engine/entity_merger.rs`

```rust
pub struct PiiMergerPattern {
    pub pattern: regex::Regex,
    pub entity_type: String,
    pub priority: i32,
    pub base_score: f32,
    pub context_boost: f32,
    pub context_words: Vec<String>,
    pub validator: Option<fn(&str) -> bool>,
}

pub struct PiiMerger {
    patterns: Vec<PiiMergerPattern>,
}

impl PiiMerger {
    pub fn new() -> Self { /* load default patterns */ }
    
    pub fn merge(&self, text: &str, entities: &[PiiMatch]) -> Vec<PiiMatch> {
        // 1. Find all regex matches
        // 2. For each match, find overlapping entities
        // 3. Merge overlapping: pick dominant label, average scores
        // 4. Add high-confidence standalone regex matches
        // 5. Return deduplicated sorted results
    }
}
```

### 2. Validators

```rust
fn validate_ssn(text: &str) -> bool;
fn validate_luhn(text: &str) -> bool;
fn validate_npi(text: &str) -> bool;
fn validate_phone_us(text: &str) -> bool;
```

### 3. Integration

Call `PiiMerger::merge()` after `NerBackendRouter::detect_all()` in the pipeline:
```
text -> regex detect -> NER backends -> merge -> entity merger -> final PiiMatch list
```

The merger runs AFTER all backends have produced their raw results, so it benefits all backends equally.

## Files to Create/Modify

- **New**: `src/engine/entity_merger.rs` — merger + patterns + validators
- **Modify**: `src/engine/detector.rs` — call merger after all detection
- **Modify**: `src/engine/mod.rs` — export module

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `PiiMerger` merges fragmented date/SSN/phone predictions correctly
- [ ] Context-aware scoring works (context words boost confidence)
- [ ] SSN validator rejects invalid patterns (000, 666, 900+ area codes)
- [ ] Luhn validator works for credit cards and NPI
- [ ] Merged results have correct character offsets
- [ ] Unit tests port from OpenMed's test cases
- [ ] Works with any backend output (not coupled to specific NER backend)
- [ ] `cargo fmt` + `cargo test` pass

## Pitfalls

- The merger operates on character offsets, not token offsets — verify alignment
- Context word matching is case-insensitive and looks in a window around the entity
- When merging fragments, the dominant label is the one with highest cumulative confidence across all merged sub-entities
- The merger can ADD entities (regex-only matches with context boost) — it's not just merging existing ones

## Dependencies

- trx-j0p5.2 (needs `PiiMatch` to be stable, should not block on other backends)

title: Perf: NER token backend loads ONNX model per chunk; batch + batch-spans for throughput
description:
# Perf: NER token backend batch + throughput

## Goal
Make nym's default NER token-classification backend dramatically faster for the
agent-session scrubbing / datatinder workload (many small chunks in one process).

## Status / Evidence (commit 8d34025)
Root cause found and fixed: decide_one() re-created the Detector (and thus
reloaded the ~138 MB ONNX model) on EVERY chunk, making --jsonl batch mode
pointless (2s per chunk was model load, not inference). Fixed by hoisting
Detector construction to once-per-process (build_decide_detector) and passing
&Detector to decide_one(). Also set with_intra_threads(available_parallelism).

Benchmarks (M2 Ultra, NER-only token backend):
- 60 tiny chunks: ~120s -> 4.1s
- 100 med chunks: ~282s -> 4.4s
- 1000 med chunks: timed out (145 done) -> 25s  (~30-80x)
Correctness intact (multilingual NER + decision output verified); 83 engine tests pass.

## Remaining work (this issue)
1. Batch multiple chunks into one padded [N, seq] forward pass in ner_token.rs
   (new detect_batch), to amortize any remaining per-call ONNX overhead across
   chunks. Cross-platform root fix.
2. Re-benchmark to confirm the batch gain.

## Proof a positive outcome
- cargo test --features decision engine:: all pass.
- time nym decide --jsonl --config <ner.toml> < <1000 chunks> completes and is at
  least ~2x faster than the current path on the same 1000 small chunks.

# Perf: CUDA / TensorRT execution provider for the NER token backend

## Goal
Wire the CUDA (and TensorRT) execution provider into nym's default NER
token-classification backend so NVIDIA boxes (4090, rtx6000) run ONNX NER on the
GPU instead of CPU.

## Background
The default token backend (ner_token.rs) used a bare Session::builder() with no
execution provider. The ner-cuda / ner-tensorrt features only accelerated the
GLiNER path via gline-rs, NOT the default token backend. Add ort/cuda (and
ort/tensorrt) to the ner-cuda / ner-tensorrt features and register the
CUDAExecutionProvider / TensorRtExecutionProvider in the token-backend session
builder under #[cfg(...)], mirroring the CoreML wiring (commit 3adcd87).

## Evidence so far (Apple Silicon, commit 3adcd87)
CoreML EP wired and working, but benchmarked SLOWER than CPU for batch-of-1 on
M2 Ultra (60 tiny chunks 4.5s CPU vs 8.0s CoreML; 1000 med chunks 25s CPU vs
CoreML timed out at 120s). Documented honestly in docs/ner-backends.md. CUDA is
expected to differ (much lower per-call overhead than CoreML) but must be
measured, not assumed.

## Proof a positive outcome
- On a CUDA box (4090 or rtx6000), build with --features ner-cuda and run:
  time nym decide --jsonl --config <ner.toml> < <1000 chunks>
  Must be faster than the CPU-only build on the same box/input, and nvidia-smi
  should show the process using the GPU during the run.

# Perf: CoreML EP for NER token backend (measured slower for batch-of-1)

## Status / Result (commit 3adcd87) - CLOSED with finding
Wired the CoreMLExecutionProvider into the NER token backend (previously
ner-coreml only accelerated GLiNER). Verified working on M2 Ultra, but measured
SLOWER than CPU for the batch-of-1 spans this CLI produces:
- 60 tiny chunks: 4.5s CPU vs 8.0s CoreML (1.8x slower)
- 1000 med chunks: 25s CPU vs CoreML timed out at 120s
Root cause: CoreML per-call overhead (lazy model conversion, ANE dispatch, graph

title: Perf: CUDA/TensorRT execution provider for NER token backend
description:

## Status (commit 736d1f0) - DONE, validated on 4090

backend (ner-cuda/ner-tensorrt features now enable ort/cuda and ort/tensorrt),
mirroring the CoreML wiring.

## Validation (RTX 4090, CUDA 12.8)
Getting the EP to actually engage was non-trivial:
- onnxruntime-gpu 1.30 requires CUDA 13 + cuDNN 9 (not present; box has CUDA 12.8)
  -> EP silently fell back to CPU.

  engages (providers: [CUDAExecutionProvider, CPUExecutionProvider]).

- 5000 medium chunks: CPU 56.4s vs CUDA 2.7s (~21x), diff outputs identical.

title: Prevent key-file overwrite and support safe cross-process replacement-map reuse
description:
Context: release-training pipelines must pseudonymize source sessions, memory snapshots and teacher targets with the same aliases. Synthetic evaluation of nym 0.2.0 and source f6bcd16a9 found that -k is output only: src/main.rs::write_key_file uses File::create; handle_anon constructs a fresh Replacer and does not reload existing mappings. The README's append-only claim does not hold for this path. A second invocation overwrites the first key file and assigns a new alias.

Reproduce offline with NER disabled and email-only detection. Input JSON contains alice@example.com followed by bob@example.com, plus an ops text referring to bob. Target JSON contains only bob@example.com. Run anon on each independently with --format json --patterns email --strategy consistent --seed 42 -k the same file. Compare bob aliases and verify the key file retains all original entries: currently aliases differ and earlier mappings disappear.

Required contract: distinguish writing a new reversible key from explicitly loading/extending an existing mapping. Do not silently destroy prior keys. Validate headers, strategy/context compatibility and conflicting entries. Use locking/atomic persistence appropriate to supported concurrency; append-only is not mandatory if safe atomic rewrite is preferable. Mappings are sensitive and must not enter public logs or artifacts.

Proof/tests: CLI integration tests in separate processes, reordered input/target detection, repeated strings across JSON fields and records, incremental new entities, restart/reload, deanon of earlier and later outputs, malformed/conflicting keys, interrupted write and concurrent extension behavior. Existing mappings must remain stable and recoverable, and invalid state must fail without truncating the original file. Run focused Rust tests, cargo check, cargo fmt, and record actual output proving the contract. Update key-file docs to match implementation.

title: Provide an explicit reproducible pseudonym context for seeded dataset builds
description:
Repeated anon invocations with the same input, config and --seed 42 produce different consistent email aliases because randomly generated session names are embedded in replacements. Source: handle_anon constructs Session and Replacer::with_session_id; replacement generation embeds that session context. A fixed RNG seed alone is not sufficient for reproducible dataset transformations.

Implement an explicit opt-in alias context/reproducible mode, coordinating with persistent mapping reuse. Define within-session versus cross-session linking policy, and preserve privacy-conscious defaults. Do not suggest an unsalted public hash as protection for guessable personal identifiers. Explain whether --seed controls replacements only or all output bytes. Keep changing timestamps/metadata out of any byte-identical transformed-content claim.

Proof/tests: two independent processes with identical explicit context/input/config/seed produce identical transformed content; distinct contexts stay intentionally separate; processing already mapped entities in a different order and adding new entities does not change existing aliases; resumed builds preserve aliases. Exercise nested JSON and linewise records. Test default nonreproducible behavior if deliberately retained. Run focused tests, cargo check and cargo fmt; document exact flags and guarantees.

title: Add JSON field/path selection with explicit coverage and structural integrity
description:
Generic JSON anonymization processes every string value, including structural UUIDs in id/parentId. Synthetic --patterns email,uuid rewrote both structural identifiers. Placeholder strategies can also collapse distinct IDs to the same token. For session/teacher datasets, role/op/fact/provenance relationships must survive while text and identifying metadata are audited.

Add explicit include/exclude field or path selection for JSON and JSONL rather than hardcoding pi's schema into nym. Define nested array/path semantics, missing selected fields, and coverage reporting. Skipped metadata is not inherently safe: users need an explicit scan/sanitize policy for it. If users opt to remap structural IDs, require a distinct referentially consistent mapping, not generic collapsing placeholders. Do not silently swallow parse errors or emit unprocessed records as though sanitized.

Proof/tests: multiple distinct id/parentId values and cross-record references remain exact under content-only selection; nested arrays, UTF-8, escapes and embedded JSON text are handled according to documented policy; selected content is redacted; input and target references stay consistent; excluded fields are reported without leaking values; malformed JSON/JSONL and mismatched selectors fail or quarantine explicitly. CLI integration tests must assert full parsed structures and valid output record counts. Run focused Rust tests, cargo check and cargo fmt.

title: Reject or honor ignored INPUT/output/format flags in anon streaming mode
description:
Synthetic reproduction: create two JSONL records with email strings. Run nym anon input.jsonl --format json --stream --no-ner --patterns email --strategy consistent --seed 42 -o output.jsonl. It exits 0, reports 0 lines and does not create output.jsonl. Redirecting stdin/stdout works. src/main.rs::handle_anon_streaming reads stdin and writes stdout via streaming::stream_anon regardless of the provided INPUT/output; it does not apply the JSON format handler. Key creation also truncates a supplied file in this path.

Choose and document supported combinations: either honor INPUT/-o/--format in stream mode or reject unsupported options clearly before any key/output side effects. Never report success for ignored file input or silently disregard requested structured handling. Preserve existing key files using the safe mapping contract; do not implement a second incompatible persistence path.

Proof/tests: file-to-file, stdin-to-stdout, file-to-stdout and stdin-to-file combinations either work as specified or reject with nonzero status. JSONL output parses record by record, record counts match, replacements persist across records, diagnostics stay on stderr, stdout contains only records, and parse/I/O/backend failures propagate. A rejected invocation must not overwrite existing output/key files. Add subprocess CLI tests and run focused tests, cargo check and cargo fmt.

title: Add opt-in audit failure policy and value-free machine-readable summaries
description:
nym detect exits 0 when findings are present, which is reasonable for inspection but not a training/CI release gate. Synthetic JSON with email, UUID, IPv4 and a fake API token demonstrated this. Detection JSON reports include matched_text, so blindly storing reports as public build artifacts would disclose the very values being audited.

Add an explicit optional fail-on policy for selected sensitive classes/patterns and unresolved decisions, with distinct documented statuses for clean pass, blocked findings and operational failure. Provide aggregate/value-free output suitable for public run manifests. Keep default inspection semantics deliberate rather than making every ordinary finding an error. Candidate caps, parse failures and unavailable required backends must not create a misleading complete/clean result. Model confidence must not be treated as automatically calibrated or as proof of safety.

Proof/tests: configured blockers return a nonzero gate status, nonblocked/clean cases succeed, execution failures are distinguishable, machine-readable output parses on all outcomes, required-backend failure never passes, and summary mode contains no original values, private source paths or reversible mappings. Exercise uncertain verdicts and incomplete scans when applicable. Run focused tests, cargo check and cargo fmt; document use in a fail-closed pipeline.

title: Benchmark nym recall and utility preservation on synthetic coding-agent session fixtures
description:

Test regex-only, locally configured NER and optional local decision backends separately. No private trace or credential should be added to git; external model calls need explicit egress approval.

Measure per-class recall/false positives and reviewed coverage, consistency across inputs/memory snapshots/targets, JSON/operation referential integrity, deterministic resume, task-relevant literal preservation, latency and failure behavior. Report denominators, false negatives and scope limits; do not declare a universal safe threshold without evidence. Cross-link mapping, streaming, selection and audit-policy issues.

Proof: a reproducible just recipe runs the offline fixture suite from a clean checkout, emits only safe aggregate results, records pinned detector/model/config versions, and fails regression assertions for seeded misses/corruption. Human-review protocol and exclusions cover proprietary content that is not reducible to PII spans; rights/consent and later weight-extraction testing remain separate checks. Run the suite and relevant tests before closing.

title: Evaluate OpenMed PII models for ONNX export
description:
## Goal

Determine which OpenMed PII token-classification models export cleanly to ONNX and benchmark them for nym's use case.

## Background

OpenMed published 33+ PII detection models on HuggingFace. These are standard HuggingFace `AutoModelForTokenClassification` models (BERT-family, ELECTRA, E5, etc.) with BIO/BIOES label schemes. Unlike the OpenAI privacy-filter which uses custom modeling code, these should export to ONNX without issues.

The models we care about are the small ones suitable for CLI use:

| HuggingFace ID | Size | Architecture |
|---|---|---|
| `OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-ClinicalE5-Small-33M-v1` | 33M | E5 (smallest) |
| `OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-SuperClinical-Small-44M-v1` | 44M | DeBERTa-v3 |
| `OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-LiteClinical-Small-66M-v1` | 66M | BERT |
| `OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-FastClinical-Small-82M-v1` | 82M | BERT |

All detect: `first_name`, `last_name`, `email`, `phone_number`, `ssn`, `date_of_birth`, `street_address`

## Steps

1. **Export to ONNX**: For each model, try exporting with `optimum-cli`:
   ```bash
   pip install optimum onnxruntime
   optimum-cli export onnx --model OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-ClinicalE5-Small-33M-v1 /tmp/onnx/clinical-e5-small
   optimum-cli export onnx --model OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-SuperClinical-Small-44M-v1 /tmp/onnx/superclinical-small
   optimum-cli export onnx --model OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-LiteClinical-Small-66M-v1 /tmp/onnx/liteclinical-small
   optimum-cli export onnx --model OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-FastClinical-Small-82M-v1 /tmp/onnx/fastclinical-small
   ```

2. **Record results**: For each model, note:
   - Did export succeed? Any custom ops?
   - ONNX file size (MB)
   - Number of labels in `id2label` (should be BIO/BIOES variants of entity types)
   - Tokenizer type (BERT tokenizer? SentencePiece? Byte-level?)

3. **Quick inference test**: Run each exported model on a test string using Python `onnxruntime`:
   ```python
   import onnxruntime as ort
   from transformers import AutoTokenizer
   
   tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-ClinicalE5-Small-33M-v1")
   session = ort.InferenceSession("/tmp/onnx/clinical-e5-small/model.onnx")
   
   text = "Patient John Smith (DOB: 01/15/1970) called from 555-123-4567 about SSN 123-45-6789"
   inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="np")
   outputs = session.run(None, dict(inputs))
   # Check shape: [1, seq_len, num_labels]
   ```

4. **Recommend a model**: Based on export success, file size, and label coverage, recommend which model to use as nym's default PII backend.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] All 4 candidate models attempted for ONNX export
- [ ] Results table: model, export success, file size, label count, tokenizer type, any issues
- [ ] Inference sanity check passed for at least 1 model
- [ ] Recommendation with rationale for which model to use in nym

## Reference

- OpenMed model registry: `openmed/core/model_registry.py` (search for the model IDs above)
- HuggingFace collection: https://huggingface.co/collections/openmed
- nym's existing ONNX infra: `src/engine/ner.rs` uses `ort` crate + `hf-hub` for downloads
close_reason: Stale: OpenMed/privacy-filter direction shelved. Regex baseline + synthetic benchmark (trx-qgdq) cover current needs; can reopen if model-backed NER is wanted.

title: Add NER backend trait and routing
description:
## Goal

Create a `NerBackend` trait in nym so multiple NER engines (GLiNER, OpenMed PII, privacy-filter) can be selected at runtime via CLI flag or config.

## Current State

nym has two hardcoded detection paths:
- `src/engine/detector.rs`: `Detector` runs regex patterns (always available)
- `src/engine/ner.rs`: `NerDetector` wraps GLiNER (feature-gated behind `ner`)

The `Detector` in `detector.rs` calls regex patterns and optionally GLiNER in sequence. There's no abstraction for swapping NER backends.

## What to Build

### 1. `NerBackend` trait in new file `src/engine/ner_backend.rs`

```rust
pub trait NerBackend {
    /// Human-readable name for CLI/config
    fn name(&self) -> &str;
    
    /// Entity types this backend can detect
    fn entity_types(&self) -> &[&str];
    
    /// Run detection, returns Vec<PiiMatch>
    fn detect(&self, text: &str) -> Result<Vec<PiiMatch>, Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>>;
}
```

### 2. Wrap existing GLiNER as `GlinerBackend`

Move the core logic from `src/engine/ner.rs::NerDetector::detect()` into a `GlinerBackend` struct that implements `NerBackend`. Keep the smart chunking, entity caching, and deduplication — they stay in GLiNER because other backends may not need them (OpenMed models handle token limits differently).

### 3. `NerBackendRouter` in `src/engine/ner_backend.rs`

```rust
pub struct NerBackendRouter {
    backends: Vec<Box<dyn NerBackend>>,
}

impl NerBackendRouter {
    pub fn new() -> Self;
    pub fn add(&mut self, backend: Box<dyn NerBackend>);
    pub fn detect_all(&self, text: &str) -> Result<Vec<PiiMatch>, ...>;
}
```

`detect_all()` runs all registered backends and merges results. Deduplication uses the same logic as `NerDetector::deduplicate_matches()` — extract that into a shared function.

### 4. CLI integration

Add to `src/main.rs` (or wherever the CLI args are):
```
--ner-backend <NAME>    Select NER backend: gliner, openmed, privacy-filter, all (default: gliner)
```

When `--ner-backend all` is used, all available backends run and results are merged.

### 5. Config integration

Add to `nym.toml`:
```toml
[ner]
backend = "gliner"       # or "openmed", "privacy-filter", "all"
model = "OpenMed/OpenMed-PII-ClinicalE5-Small-33M-v1"  # model-specific override
threshold = 0.5
```

## Files to Modify

- **New**: `src/engine/ner_backend.rs` — trait + router
- **Modify**: `src/engine/ner.rs` — extract `GlinerBackend` impl, keep `NerDetector` as thin wrapper
- **Modify**: `src/engine/detector.rs` — use `NerBackendRouter` instead of direct `NerDetector`
- **Modify**: `src/engine/mod.rs` — export new module
- **Modify**: `src/main.rs` (or CLI module) — add `--ner-backend` flag
- **Modify**: `src/config.rs` — add `[ner]` section parsing

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `NerBackend` trait defined with `name()`, `entity_types()`, `detect()`
- [ ] Existing GLiNER wrapped as `GlinerBackend` implementing the trait
- [ ] `NerBackendRouter` runs 1 or N backends and deduplicates
- [ ] `--ner-backend` CLI flag works
- [ ] Config `[ner]` section parsed
- [ ] All existing tests pass (no behavior change for default GLiNER backend)
- [ ] `cargo fmt` + `cargo test` pass

## Pitfalls

- Don't break the existing `ner` feature gate — `GlinerBackend` must still be `#[cfg(feature = "ner")]`
- The macOS ONNX crash workaround in `ner.rs` must remain — it applies to all ONNX-based backends
- `PiiMatch` struct in `detector.rs` must work for all backends without modification

title: Implement OpenAI privacy-filter backend with Viterbi decoding
description:
## Goal

Add a `PrivacyFilterBackend` that implements `NerBackend` and runs the OpenAI privacy-filter model (and its Nemotron fine-tune) with BIOES-constrained Viterbi decoding in Rust.

## Background

The OpenAI privacy-filter (`openai/privacy-filter`) is a custom MoE token classifier that requires:
1. **Custom modeling code** (`modeling_openai_privacy_filter.py` in the HF repo) — this is NOT a standard HuggingFace model
2. **BIOES-constrained Viterbi decoding** with 6 learned transition biases
3. **Span post-processing** to tighten overly greedy boundaries

OpenMed also published a Nemotron fine-tune: `OpenMed/privacy-filter-nemotron`

This is the most complex backend because of the Viterbi decoder and the custom model architecture.

## Reference Implementation (Python)

Study these files from github.com/maziyarpanahi/openmed:

### `openmed/core/decoding/viterbi.py` (~200 lines)
Pure-Python BIOES Viterbi decoder. Key components:
- `TokenLabelInfo`: Resolves `id2label` into BIOES tag/span-label tables
  - `span_class_names`: `["O", "NAME", "EMAIL", ...]`
  - `token_boundary_tags`: `{label_id: "B"|"I"|"E"|"S"|None}`
  - `token_to_span_label`: `{label_id: span_index}`
- `viterbi_decode(token_logprobs, label_info, biases)`: Main decoder
  - Builds start/end/transition score matrices from the 6 biases
  - Runs standard Viterbi with backpointers
  - Enforces BIOES state machine (e.g. B-X can only continue to I-X or E-X)
- `VITERBI_BIAS_KEYS`: 6 learned biases:
  - `transition_bias_background_stay`
  - `transition_bias_background_to_start`
  - `transition_bias_inside_to_continue`
  - `transition_bias_inside_to_end`
  - `transition_bias_end_to_background`
  - `transition_bias_end_to_start`

### `openmed/core/decoding/spans.py` (~80 lines)
- `trim_span_whitespace(start, end, text)` — strip leading/trailing whitespace
- `refine_privacy_filter_span(label, start, end, text)` — tighten spans:
  - For email/URL/phone labels: find strict regex match inside model span
  - For all labels: strip trailing " and" / " or" that model absorbs

### `openmed/torch/privacy_filter.py` (~130 lines)
- Uses `AutoModelForTokenClassification` with `trust_remote_code=True`
- Outputs normalized entity dicts: `{entity_group, score, word, start, end}`
- Calls `refine_privacy_filter_span` on each result

## What to Build

### 1. Rust Viterbi decoder in `src/engine/viterbi.rs`

Direct port of `viterbi.py`. Key structs:

```rust
pub struct TokenLabelInfo {
    pub span_class_names: Vec<String>,
    pub span_label_lookup: HashMap<String, usize>,
    pub token_to_span_label: HashMap<usize, usize>,
    pub token_boundary_tags: HashMap<usize, Option<char>>, // 'B','I','E','S',None
    pub background_token_label: usize,
    pub background_span_label: usize,
}

pub struct ViterbiBiases {
    pub background_stay: f32,
    pub background_to_start: f32,
    pub inside_to_continue: f32,
    pub inside_to_end: f32,
    pub end_to_background: f32,
    pub end_to_start: f32,
}

pub fn viterbi_decode(
    token_logprobs: &[Vec<f32>],  // [seq_len][num_classes]
    label_info: &TokenLabelInfo,
    biases: &ViterbiBiases,
) -> Vec<usize>  // predicted class indices
```

### 2. Span post-processing in `src/engine/span_utils.rs`

Port of `spans.py`:

```rust
pub fn trim_span_whitespace(start: usize, end: usize, text: &str) -> (usize, usize);
pub fn refine_privacy_filter_span(label: &str, start: usize, end: usize, text: &str) -> (usize, usize);
```

### 3. `PrivacyFilterBackend` in `src/engine/privacy_filter_backend.rs`

```rust
pub struct PrivacyFilterBackend {
    session: ort::Session,
    tokenizer: tokenizers::Tokenizer,
    label_info: TokenLabelInfo,
    biases: ViterbiBiases,  // loaded from model config
    threshold: f32,
}

impl NerBackend for PrivacyFilterBackend {
    fn name(&self) -> &str { "privacy-filter" }
    
    fn detect(&self, text: &str) -> Result<Vec<PiiMatch>, ...> {
        // 1. Tokenize
        // 2. ONNX inference -> logits
        // 3. Apply log-softmax to get log-probs
        // 4. viterbi_decode(log_probs, label_info, biases)
        // 5. labels_to_token_spans() -> (label, start, end) triples
        // 6. Map token spans to char offsets
        // 7. Apply refine_privacy_filter_span to each
        // 8. Convert to PiiMatch
    }
}
```

### 4. ONNX export challenge

The privacy-filter uses custom modeling code. Two approaches:

**Option A**: Export to ONNX with `trust_remote_code=True`:
```bash
optimum-cli export onnx --model openai/privacy-filter --trust-remote-code /tmp/onnx/privacy-filter
```
This may or may not work depending on whether the custom ops are ONNX-compatible.

**Option B**: If ONNX export fails, we need to understand the model architecture enough to either:
- Pre-export the ONNX artifacts from Python and host them on HF
- Or use the `candle` crate for native Rust inference

Investigate Option A first.

### 5. Transition bias loading

The 6 Viterbi biases are stored in the model's config.json under keys matching `VITERBI_BIAS_KEYS`. Parse them during construction:

```rust
let biases = ViterbiBiases {
    background_stay: config["transition_bias_background_stay"].as_f64().unwrap_or(0.0) as f32,
    // ... etc
};
```

## Files to Create/Modify

- **New**: `src/engine/viterbi.rs` — BIOES Viterbi decoder
- **New**: `src/engine/span_utils.rs` — Span post-processing
- **New**: `src/engine/privacy_filter_backend.rs` — Backend implementation

- [ ] Results match Python implementation on same input (within floating-point tolerance)

- The privacy-filter model uses `trust_remote_code` — ONNX export may fail or produce custom ops that `ort` can't run. Test this early.
- Viterbi needs `log_softmax` applied to raw logits before decoding — don't forget this step

title: Port OpenMed smart entity merger for cross-backend dedup
description:
## Goal

Port OpenMed's regex-based semantic entity merger to Rust. This post-processes NER output from ANY backend to merge fragmented predictions into coherent entities.

## Problem

Token classifiers often split semantic PII units across multiple predictions:
```
Model raw output:
  [date] '01' (0.71)
  [date_of_birth] '/15/1970' (0.75)

Expected:
  [date_of_birth] '01/15/1970' (0.73)
```

This happens because tokenizers split strings like `01/15/1970` into sub-tokens and the model may assign different labels to different pieces.

## Reference Implementation

`openmed/core/pii_entity_merger.py` (~350 lines). Key concepts:

### `PIIPattern` struct
Each pattern has:
- `pattern`: Regex for the semantic unit
- `entity_type`: Target label (e.g. "ssn", "phone_number")
- `priority`: Higher = checked first
- `base_score`: Confidence without context (0.01-0.9)
- `context_boost`: Extra confidence when context words found nearby (0.1-0.65)
- `context_words`: Keywords that boost confidence (e.g. ["ssn", "social security"])
- `validator`: Optional function (SSN checksum, Luhn, NPI validation, phone format)

### `merge_entities_with_semantic_units()`
1. Find all regex pattern matches in text
2. For each match, check if it overlaps with model predictions
3. If overlapping: merge fragments, use dominant label (highest cumulative score)
4. If no overlap but high confidence (base + context): add as new entity

### Validators
- `validate_ssn()`: SSN rules (no 000 groups, no 666 area, no 900-999)
- `validate_luhn()`: Credit card Luhn algorithm
- `validate_npi()`: NPI with 80840 prefix Luhn
- `validate_phone_us()`: US phone format checks

### Pattern catalog
- Dates: ISO, US, European, spelled-out months
- SSN: `XXX-XX-XXXX`, `XXX XX XXXX`
- Phone: `(XXX) XXX-XXXX`, `XXX-XXX-XXXX`, 10-digit
- Email: standard pattern
- ZIP: 5-digit, ZIP+4
- Credit card: 4x4 groups with Luhn
- MRN: `MRN:XXXXXX`, `ABX123456`
- Street address: number + street + suffix
- NPI: 10-digit with Luhn

## What to Build

### 1. `PiiMergerPattern` and `PiiMerger` in `src/engine/entity_merger.rs`

```rust
pub struct PiiMergerPattern {
    pub pattern: regex::Regex,
    pub entity_type: String,
    pub priority: i32,
    pub base_score: f32,
    pub context_boost: f32,
    pub context_words: Vec<String>,
    pub validator: Option<fn(&str) -> bool>,
}

pub struct PiiMerger {
    patterns: Vec<PiiMergerPattern>,
}

impl PiiMerger {
    pub fn new() -> Self { /* load default patterns */ }
    
    pub fn merge(&self, text: &str, entities: &[PiiMatch]) -> Vec<PiiMatch> {
        // 1. Find all regex matches
        // 2. For each match, find overlapping entities
        // 3. Merge overlapping: pick dominant label, average scores
        // 4. Add high-confidence standalone regex matches
        // 5. Return deduplicated sorted results
    }
}
```

### 2. Validators

```rust
fn validate_ssn(text: &str) -> bool;
fn validate_luhn(text: &str) -> bool;
fn validate_npi(text: &str) -> bool;
fn validate_phone_us(text: &str) -> bool;
```

### 3. Integration

Call `PiiMerger::merge()` after `NerBackendRouter::detect_all()` in the pipeline:
```
text -> regex detect -> NER backends -> merge -> entity merger -> final PiiMatch list
```

The merger runs AFTER all backends have produced their raw results, so it benefits all backends equally.

## Files to Create/Modify

- **New**: `src/engine/entity_merger.rs` — merger + patterns + validators
- **Modify**: `src/engine/detector.rs` — call merger after all detection
- **Modify**: `src/engine/mod.rs` — export module

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `PiiMerger` merges fragmented date/SSN/phone predictions correctly
- [ ] Context-aware scoring works (context words boost confidence)
- [ ] SSN validator rejects invalid patterns (000, 666, 900+ area codes)
- [ ] Luhn validator works for credit cards and NPI
- [ ] Merged results have correct character offsets
- [ ] Unit tests port from OpenMed's test cases
- [ ] Works with any backend output (not coupled to specific NER backend)
- [ ] `cargo fmt` + `cargo test` pass

## Pitfalls

- The merger operates on character offsets, not token offsets — verify alignment
- Context word matching is case-insensitive and looks in a window around the entity
- When merging fragments, the dominant label is the one with highest cumulative confidence across all merged sub-entities
- The merger can ADD entities (regex-only matches with context boost) — it's not just merging existing ones

## Dependencies

- trx-j0p5.2 (needs `PiiMatch` to be stable, should not block on other backends)

title: OpenMed + privacy-filter NER backends
description:
## Context

OpenMed (github.com/maziyarpanahi/openmed, Apache 2.0) is a medical NLP toolkit with 33+ PII token-classification models and an integration of OpenAI's `openai/privacy-filter` model. Both are directly usable by nym for PII detection beyond regex + GLiNER.

nym currently has two detection paths:
1. **Regex** (`src/engine/patterns.rs`, `src/engine/detector.rs`) — fast, deterministic, no deps
2. **GLiNER NER** (`src/engine/ner.rs`, feature-gated behind `ner`) — zero-shot ONNX model via `gline-rs` + `ort` + `hf-hub`

This epic adds two new NER backends:
- **OpenMed PII models**: Standard HuggingFace token-classification (BIO/BIOES tagging). Small models (33M-82M params) export cleanly to ONNX. Purpose-trained for PII detection on clinical data; will outperform GLiNER for this specific task.
- **OpenAI privacy-filter** (original `openai/privacy-filter` + OpenMed's Nemotron fine-tune `OpenMed/privacy-filter-nemotron`): Custom MoE architecture with Viterbi decoding. More complex but higher quality on structured PII.

## Reference: OpenMed source files to study

All paths relative to github.com/maziyarpanahi/openmed:
- `openmed/core/backends.py` — Backend routing (MLX vs Torch), privacy-filter dispatcher
- `openmed/core/pii.py` — PII extraction pipeline, model family detection, accent normalization
- `openmed/core/pii_entity_merger.py` — Regex-based semantic unit merging with context-aware scoring (Presidio-inspired), validators (SSN Luhn, NPI, phone)
- `openmed/core/pii_i18n.py` — Language-specific patterns and default models
- `openmed/core/decoding/viterbi.py` — BIOES-constrained Viterbi decoder, TokenLabelInfo, transition bias handling
- `openmed/core/decoding/spans.py` — Span post-processing (trim whitespace, tighten email/URL/phone spans)
- `openmed/core/model_registry.py` — Full model catalog with sizes, entity types, confidence thresholds
- `openmed/torch/privacy_filter.py` — PyTorch wrapper for privacy-filter with trust_remote_code

title: recursive ** wildcard for JSON path selectors
description: Found while verifying README examples for trx-dw3c: PathPattern's * wildcard matches exactly one path segment, so excluding 'all ids at any depth' requires listing every depth explicitly (messages.*.id, meta.id, ...). A recursive '**' segment (matches zero or more segments) would make --exclude-path '**.id' work in one pattern. Proof: nym detect on {"messages":[{"id":...}],"meta":{"id":...}} with --exclude-path '**.id' skips both ids; --json-coverage reports both under skipped; existing tests in src/engine/selector.rs still pass; add unit tests for '**' at start/middle/end.
